newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Meridor defends capital market reform.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Meridor defends capital market reform.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor on Monday defended a proposed tax on savings as part of capital market reform, saying it was "just for society and more right for the capital market".
The cabinet decided early on Monday morning to postpone a decision on a politically sensitive tax on short-term savings that was a key component of the proposed reform.
"Yesterday was a not a good day for the government or for the capital market," he said in remarks broadcast on Israel Radio. "I am not accustomed to criticising the government in public."

The comment was made in response to a reporter's question as to whether Meridor could continue to serve in a government in which he does not have the support of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Meridor did not directly respond to the question.

"The report we (the Treasury) put forward is balanced, moderate and does not at all increase taxation. It just has a different division of tax benefits. In a way that is more just for society and more right for the capital markets."
"I hope that in the coming days everyone will reach the same conclusion," he said.
The Finance Ministry's proposal aims to encourage long-term savings by imposing a tax on shorter term alternatives. It also expands tax benefits for long-term instruments such as pension funds.
Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel, who opposed the short-term savings tax, said he thought the partial adoption of the proposal was a "positive and good development".
